name: Place Assarag
hero_subtitle: Taroudant's main square: café terraces, local life and the doorway to both souks in the Little Marrakech.

overview.title: A square that sets the pace of the day
overview.p1: Place Assarag (also known as Place al-Alaouiyine) is the social centre of Taroudant, the Little Marrakech of the Souss. It sits between the Arab souk and the Berber souk and is the natural place to orient yourself, order mint tea and watch the city move.
overview.p2: In the morning the square is calm: a few café tables, shopkeepers opening shutters, the occasional calèche. By late afternoon locals gather for coffee or juice, and the lanes leading into both markets fill with everyday trade rather than heavy tourist traffic.
overview.p3: It is not a monumental square in the European sense. Its value is practical and human: a clear landmark for taxis and walkers, a place to rest between markets, and a window onto the slower rhythm of a Souss Valley market town.

moods.title: Place Assarag through the day
moods.subtitle: Three different atmospheres on the same square.

1.title: Quiet coffee and orientation
1.desc: Fresh orange juice or coffee at a pavement café, then a first look at the lanes into the souks before the day heats up.

2.title: Local life and golden light
2.desc: Tables fill, conversations rise, and the square becomes the natural meeting point between the two markets.

3.title: Terrace time after the markets
3.desc: A last mint tea or a simple dinner facing the square before walking back toward the ramparts or your riad.

food.title: What to eat near the square
food.p1: Several cafés and simple restaurants face the square. For a fuller meal, step into the nearby Arab or Berber souk, or book a table in a medina riad. Prices are usually lower and less pressured than in larger tourist cities.
food.li1: Mint tea and fresh orange juice on a café terrace overlooking the square.
food.li2: Simple Moroccan staples — tagine, couscous or grilled meats — in square-side restaurants.
food.li3: Argan oil, amlou and local honey from stalls in the nearby souks.
food.li4: Pastries and coffee at a local café before or after shopping.
food.li5: A quiet dinner in a riad courtyard a few minutes’ walk from the square.
food.p2: Check prices before ordering in simple restaurants. If you prefer a guide for a first meal, a short food walk is an easy option.

1.title: How to arrive
1.desc: Most taxis and walking routes meet at or near the square. It is an easy landmark to name for a driver. Petit taxis should use the meter; grands taxis and calèches need a fixed price agreed in advance.

2.title: Photos and vendors
2.desc: People-watching is part of the experience. If you photograph shopkeepers, ask first. Unofficial guides may offer to lead you into the souks; a firm “no thank you” is enough.

3.title: Stay comfortable
3.desc: Keep bags in front of you in denser moments and avoid leaving phones on café tables unattended. The square itself is open and straightforward to leave in any direction.

q1.question: Is Place Assarag free to visit?
q1.answer: Yes. There is no ticket and no gate. The square is open at all hours. You only pay for drinks at the cafés or purchases in the surrounding souks.

q2.question: What is the best time to go to Place Assarag?
q2.answer: Morning for a quiet coffee and orientation, late afternoon into the evening for the busiest local atmosphere. The square stays active after dark with café terraces.

q3.question: Is Place Assarag safe at night?
q3.answer: Most visitors feel comfortable. The square is well lit and busy with locals. Keep valuables secure as you would in any public space.

q4.question: How long should I spend at Place Assarag?
q4.answer: Plan on 30 minutes to 1.5 hours for a drink and people-watching. Use it as a base between the Arab and Berber souks and you may return several times in a day.

q5.question: Can I eat at Place Assarag?
q5.answer: Yes. Several cafés and simple restaurants face the square. For a fuller meal, step into the nearby souks or book a table in a medina riad.
